neighbours.label: long-distance commerce in historical narrative: trade routes, trading centres, merchants and caravans linking regions
fire: In the Middle Ages, Genoese merchants dominated the trade routes of the Black Sea.
Arab dhows carried ivory and gold along the trading ports of the Swahili coast.
The Hanseatic League controlled commerce between the Baltic towns.
Phoenician traders sailed from Tyre to Spain to exchange tin and dye.
The kingdom grew rich from the caravan trade in gold and salt.
Portuguese ships opened a sea route for the spice trade with India.
Sogdian merchants linked the oasis cities along the Silk Road.
Malacca became the chief trading centre of the Straits.
quiet: In the Middle Ages, Genoese admirals fought wars on the Black Sea.
Arab scholars wrote poems and histories in the coastal towns of the Swahili coast.
The Hanseatic towns built tall brick churches along the Baltic.
Phoenician sailors founded colonies far from Tyre in Spain.
The kingdom grew powerful from its large army of cavalry.
Portuguese ships explored the African coast in search of glory.
Buddhist monks built temples in the oasis cities of Central Asia.
Malacca was ruled by a sultan for over a century.
